flashcards.front: Which IPsec protocol provides confidentiality?
flashcards.back: ESP (protocol 50); AH (protocol 51) only provides integrity and authentication.

flashcards.front: What is an IPsec Security Association and how is it identified?
flashcards.back: A one-way set of agreed algorithms and keys between peers, identified by SPI, destination IP and protocol.

flashcards.front: Name the main TLS 1.2 handshake messages in order.
flashcards.back: ClientHello, ServerHello, Certificate, (ServerKeyExchange), ServerHelloDone, ClientKeyExchange, ChangeCipherSpec, Finished from both sides.

flashcards.front: Site-to-site vs remote-access VPN?
flashcards.back: Site-to-site links whole networks through gateways; remote access connects a single user's device to the private network.

questions.questionText: Which IPsec protocol provides encryption of the payload?
options: AH
IKE
ESP
ISAKMP
questions.explanation: ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) provides confidentiality plus optional integrity; AH gives integrity and authentication only.

questions.questionText: In which IPsec mode is the entire original IP packet encapsulated and given a new IP header?
options: Transport mode
Tunnel mode
Main mode
Aggressive mode
questions.explanation: Tunnel mode protects the whole original packet inside a new outer header and is used by site-to-site VPN gateways; main and aggressive are IKE phase-1 modes.

questions.questionText: How many round trips does a full TLS 1.3 handshake take before application data can be sent (excluding TCP setup)?
options: 0 in every case
questions.explanation: TLS 1.3 completes a full handshake in 1 RTT versus 2 RTT for TLS 1.2; 0-RTT is possible only when resuming a previous session.

questions.questionText: What does VPN stand for?
options: Virtual Private Network
Very Private Network
Virtual Public Network
Verified Private Network
questions.explanation: A VPN is a virtual private network: an encrypted tunnel across a shared public network that lets remote hosts or sites behave as if they were on one private network.

questions.questionText: Which of the following best describes a VPN?
options: A hardware firewall that blocks incoming connections
A secure, encrypted connection (a tunnel) across an untrusted network such as the Internet
A DNS resolution service
A peer-to-peer file-sharing protocol
questions.explanation: A VPN wraps private traffic in encrypted, authenticated packets so that it can cross the Internet safely; IPsec and TLS-based VPNs are the common types. A firewall may terminate VPN tunnels, but it is not itself a VPN.

questions.questionText: At which layer does IPsec provide security?
options: Application layer
Transport layer
Network layer
Physical layer
questions.explanation: IPsec protects the IP packets themselves, so TCP, UDP, ICMP and every application above them are covered without any change to the applications. TLS, by contrast, sits above TCP and protects one connection at a time.

questions.questionText: Which protocol suite is most commonly used to build secure site-to-site VPNs between the gateways of two offices?
options: FTP
BGP
SMTP
IPsec
questions.explanation: IPsec, with ESP in tunnel mode and IKE for key exchange, is the standard for gateway-to-gateway VPNs. FTP transfers files, BGP exchanges routes between autonomous systems and SMTP carries e-mail, and none of them provides this security.

questions.questionText: What does SSL/TLS add to a TCP connection?
options: Authentication of the server (and optionally the client), plus encryption and integrity protection of the data
Packet sequencing and retransmission of lost segments
Bandwidth reservation along the path
Flow control between the sender and the receiver
questions.explanation: TLS adds the security services: certificate-based authentication, confidentiality and integrity. Sequencing, retransmission and flow control are already done by TCP underneath, and SSL itself is obsolete, so today this means TLS 1.2 or 1.3.

questions.questionText: Which statement about SSL and TLS is correct today?
options: SSL 3.0 is newer and stronger than TLS 1.2
All SSL versions, and also TLS 1.0 and 1.1, are deprecated; secure connections should use TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3
HTTPS still requires SSL 3.0 for compatibility
SSL and TLS are unrelated protocols with different purposes
questions.explanation: TLS 1.0 (1999) was the IETF's successor to Netscape's SSL 3.0. SSL 2.0 and 3.0 are prohibited (RFC 6176 and RFC 7568; POODLE broke SSL 3.0), and RFC 8996 deprecated TLS 1.0 and 1.1 in 2021.

questions.questionText: Which transport protocol and port does IKE use to negotiate IPsec security associations when there is no NAT on the path?
options: TCP port 443
UDP port 53
UDP port 500
TCP port 22
questions.explanation: IKE runs over UDP port 500; when a NAT is detected, IKE and ESP move to UDP port 4500 (NAT traversal). Port 443 is HTTPS, 53 is DNS and 22 is SSH.

questions.questionText: What does the STARTTLS command do in SMTP, IMAP and POP3?
options: It upgrades a connection that began in plain text on the protocol's normal port to TLS, before any credentials or message data are sent
It opens a second connection on a dedicated TLS-only port
It encrypts the message end to end, so that no mail server can read it
It starts an IPsec tunnel between the two mail servers
questions.explanation: With STARTTLS the two sides first talk in clear (for example SMTP on port 587 or 25) and then run the TLS handshake on the same connection. It protects only that hop, and an active attacker who strips the STARTTLS offer can force plain text unless TLS is required.

questions.questionText: TLS needs a reliable, in-order byte stream and therefore runs over TCP. Which protocol gives the same kind of security to UDP-based applications, such as WebRTC or some VPN clients?
options: SSH
S/MIME
DTLS (Datagram TLS)
L2TP
questions.explanation: DTLS adapts TLS to datagrams by adding explicit sequence numbers and coping with loss and reordering itself. SSH secures remote logins over TCP, S/MIME secures e-mail messages, and L2TP is a tunnelling protocol with no encryption of its own.

questions.questionText: Which option correctly matches each security protocol with the layer at which it protects traffic?
options: IPsec: transport layer; TLS: network layer; WPA2: application layer; PGP: data link layer
IPsec: data link layer; TLS: application layer; WPA2: network layer; PGP: transport layer
IPsec: network layer; TLS: data link layer; WPA2: physical layer; PGP: transport layer
IPsec: network layer; TLS: just above TCP, below the application; WPA2: data link layer (Wi-Fi); PGP: application layer
questions.explanation: IPsec protects IP packets, TLS protects a TCP byte stream just above the transport layer, WPA2 encrypts Wi-Fi frames at the data link layer, and PGP protects the message itself at the application layer. Lower-layer protection covers all traffic between two points, while higher-layer protection travels end to end with the data.

questions.questionText: An attacker records many TLS 1.2 sessions with a server and, years later, steals the server's RSA private key. Which of the recorded sessions can he now decrypt?
options: Every recorded session, whatever key exchange was used
None, because TLS never uses the certificate's key for anything
Only the sessions that used ECDHE key exchange
The sessions that used RSA key transport, in which the client encrypted the pre-master secret with the server's RSA public key; sessions that used ephemeral (EC)DHE stay safe
questions.explanation: With RSA key transport the stolen key decrypts the recorded pre-master secret and hence every session key. With ephemeral (EC)DHE the RSA key only signs the handshake and the DH secrets are discarded, which is forward secrecy; TLS 1.3 therefore allows only (EC)DHE.

questions.questionText: Which of the following was removed from TLS in version 1.3?
options: AES-GCM authenticated encryption
Static RSA key transport, in which the client encrypts a pre-master secret with the server's RSA public key
Ephemeral elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange
X.509 certificates for server authentication
questions.explanation: TLS 1.3 removed static RSA and static DH key exchange, CBC and RC4 ciphers, compression and renegotiation, keeping only AEAD ciphers and (EC)DHE. Certificates are still used, but only to sign the handshake.

questions.questionText: In the TLS 1.2 cipher suite TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, which component authenticates the server?
options: ECDHE
AES_256_GCM
SHA384
ECDSA, the signature algorithm of the key in the server's certificate
questions.explanation: The server signs its ephemeral ECDHE parameters with the ECDSA private key that matches its certificate, which proves its identity. ECDHE agrees the keys, AES-256-GCM encrypts and authenticates the records, and SHA-384 is the hash used by the key-derivation function (PRF).

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the Finished messages at the end of a TLS handshake?
options: They close the TCP connection once the handshake is over
Each side sends a MAC, computed with the new keys, over the entire handshake transcript, so that any tampering with earlier handshake messages, such as a cipher-suite downgrade, is detected
They carry the server's certificate chain
They tell the certificate authority that the session has started
questions.explanation: The hello messages travel before any keys exist, so an attacker could try to alter them; the Finished messages prove that both sides saw the same handshake and hold the same keys. Without 0-RTT or False Start, the client sends application data only after it has verified the server's Finished.

questions.questionText: On public Wi-Fi an attacker intercepts a user's connection to https://bank.example and presents his own self-signed certificate for bank.example. What normally defeats this attack?
options: Nothing needs to, because TLS encryption alone stops the attacker from reading the data
The TCP checksum detects the forged certificate

The browser cannot chain the certificate to a trusted root CA, so it shows an error and does not continue; the attack works only if the user clicks through the warning or a rogue root certificate has been installed
The access point's WPA2 encryption blocks the attacker's certificate
questions.explanation: The attacker terminates the TLS connection himself, so encryption alone would protect nothing; it is the certificate check that ties the keys to the real bank. HSTS makes browsers refuse to let users click through such errors on sites that use it.

questions.questionText: Why does IPsec AH fail when a NAT device sits between the two peers, while ESP with NAT traversal works?
options: AH packets are larger than the NAT device's MTU
NAT devices drop every encrypted packet

AH's integrity check covers the addresses in the outer IP header, which NAT rewrites, so the check fails; ESP does not authenticate the outer header, and NAT traversal wraps ESP in UDP port 4500 so that the NAT has ports to translate
AH runs over TCP, which NAT cannot translate
questions.explanation: AH authenticates the unchanging fields of the IP header, including the addresses, so any address translation makes every packet look forged. ESP's ICV covers only the ESP header, payload and trailer, and the UDP wrapper gives the NAT a port pair to work with.

questions.questionText: Two IPsec gateways exchange ESP-protected traffic in both directions. How many ESP security associations do they need, and how does a receiver find the SA an arriving packet belongs to?
options: Two SAs, one for each direction; the receiver finds the SA from the SPI in the ESP header (together with the destination address and protocol)
One SA, found from the pair of IP addresses
Four SAs, one per host and direction, found from the TCP port numbers
Two SAs, found from the IKE port number 500
questions.explanation: An SA is one-way, so two-way traffic needs a pair, each with its own SPI chosen by the receiving side. The receiver looks the SPI up in its Security Association Database to get the keys and algorithms for that packet.

questions.questionText: An observer on the Internet captures a packet of a site-to-site VPN that uses ESP in tunnel mode. What can he read?
options: The inner hosts' IP addresses and TCP port numbers, but not the data
Nothing at all, not even the outer IP header
The two gateways' IP addresses, the SPI, the sequence number and the packet's length, but not the inner addresses, the port numbers or the data
Everything, because ESP in tunnel mode only authenticates the packet
questions.explanation: The new outer IP header and the ESP header (SPI and sequence number) must stay in clear for routing and SA lookup, while the whole original packet, including its header and ports, is encrypted. Only the size and timing of packets still leak, which allows limited traffic analysis.

questions.questionText: In IKEv2, what happens in the first two exchanges, IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH?
options: IKE_SA_INIT sends each peer's password in clear, and IKE_AUTH checks it against a RADIUS server

IKE_SA_INIT negotiates algorithms and runs a Diffie-Hellman exchange with nonces to create the IKE SA; IKE_AUTH then authenticates the peers (with certificates or a pre-shared key) under that protection and sets up the first child SA for ESP or AH
IKE_SA_INIT creates the ESP SA directly, without any Diffie-Hellman exchange
Both exchanges are TCP handshakes on port 443
questions.explanation: The four messages (two round trips) first establish shared keys and then prove identities inside the encrypted IKE SA, so the identities are hidden from passive observers. Further child SAs and rekeying use CREATE_CHILD_SA exchanges (RFC 7296).

questions.questionText: A company links its Kathmandu and Pokhara offices over the Internet so that any host at one site can reach any host at the other, with the two gateways doing all the encryption. Which IPsec configuration fits best?
options: AH in transport mode between every pair of hosts
ESP in transport mode between the two gateways only
AH in tunnel mode, because AH encrypts the whole packet
ESP in tunnel mode between the two gateways, as a site-to-site VPN
questions.explanation: Tunnel mode lets the gateways wrap every packet between the sites in a new header addressed gateway to gateway, so the hosts need no IPsec software, and ESP supplies the encryption. Transport mode between the gateways would protect only traffic addressed to the gateways themselves, and AH never encrypts.

questions.questionText: A salesperson's IPsec VPN client often fails on hotel networks, while the company's SSL/TLS VPN client works there. What is the most likely reason?
options: The SSL/TLS VPN does not encrypt the traffic, so the hotel firewall lets it through
IPsec works only over IPv6
The SSL/TLS VPN uses TCP port 22, which hotels always open
The SSL/TLS VPN runs over port 443 like ordinary HTTPS, which hotel firewalls and NATs almost always allow, whereas IPsec needs UDP 500 and 4500 or IP protocol 50, which are often blocked
questions.explanation: Guest networks usually allow web traffic but may block other ports and protocols, and plain ESP has no ports for a NAT to translate. A TLS-based VPN looks like HTTPS to the network and so gets through, while still encrypting everything inside the tunnel.

questions.questionText: A traveller connects to a commercial VPN service before browsing on hotel Wi-Fi. Which statement is correct?
options: No one, including the VPN provider, can see which sites the traveller visits

The hotel network sees only encrypted traffic to the VPN server and websites see the VPN server's address, but the VPN provider can see the traffic leaving its server, so the traveller must trust the provider
Websites still see the traveller's hotel IP address
HTTPS is no longer needed, because the VPN encrypts the traffic all the way to each website
questions.explanation: The tunnel ends at the VPN server, which decrypts and forwards the traffic, so beyond it the data is protected only by what the application itself uses, such as HTTPS. A VPN therefore moves trust from the local network to the VPN provider rather than removing it.

questions.questionText: What does the 8-byte ESP header that follows the IP header contain?
options: The 32-bit Security Parameter Index (SPI) and the 32-bit sequence number
The source and destination port numbers
The Pad Length and Next Header fields
The initialisation vector and the integrity check value
questions.explanation: The SPI identifies the SA and the sequence number provides anti-replay protection. Padding, Pad Length and Next Header form the encrypted ESP trailer, the IV (when the cipher needs one) starts the payload, and the ICV comes last.

questions.questionText: IPsec AH in transport mode with HMAC-SHA1-96 is applied to a 1,000-byte IPv4 packet. The AH header has 12 bytes of fixed fields (Next Header, Payload Length, Reserved, SPI, Sequence Number) followed by the 96-bit ICV. What is the size of the protected packet?
options: 1,012 bytes
1,044 bytes
1,024 bytes
1,108 bytes
questions.explanation: The ICV is 96 / 8 = 12 bytes, so AH adds 12 + 12 = 24 bytes and transport mode keeps the original IP header: 1,000 + 24 = 1,024 bytes. 1,012 forgets the ICV, 1,044 adds a new 20-byte IP header as in tunnel mode, and 1,108 counts the ICV as 96 bytes.

questions.questionText: The RTT between a client and a server is 60 ms; processing and transmission times are ignored, and neither TLS False Start nor 0-RTT is used. Counting from the moment the client sends its TCP SYN, when can the client send its first byte of application data with (i) a full TLS 1.2 handshake, (ii) a resumed TLS 1.2 session (abbreviated handshake) and (iii) a full TLS 1.3 handshake?
options: (i) 180 ms, (ii) 120 ms, (iii) 120 ms
(i) 120 ms, (ii) 60 ms, (iii) 60 ms
(i) 180 ms, (ii) 180 ms, (iii) 120 ms
(i) 180 ms, (ii) 120 ms, (iii) 60 ms
questions.explanation: TCP takes 1 RTT (60 ms), after which the ClientHello goes out. A full TLS 1.2 handshake then needs 2 more RTTs (180 ms), while an abbreviated TLS 1.2 resumption and a full TLS 1.3 handshake each need 1 (120 ms); only TLS 1.3 0-RTT resumption could send data with the ClientHello at 60 ms.

questions.questionText: A gateway protects a 1,000-byte IPv4 packet with ESP in tunnel mode, using AES-CBC (16-byte IV, 16-byte blocks) and HMAC-SHA-256-128 (16-byte ICV). The encrypted part (inner packet, padding, 1-byte Pad Length and 1-byte Next Header) must be a whole number of blocks. How long is the resulting packet, including the new 20-byte IPv4 header?
options: 1,062 bytes
1,048 bytes
1,052 bytes
1,068 bytes
questions.explanation: Encrypted part: 1,000 + 2 = 1,002 bytes, padded up to 1,008 (63 blocks, 6 padding bytes); total = 20 (new IP) + 8 (SPI and sequence) + 16 (IV) + 1,008 + 16 (ICV) = 1,068 bytes. 1,062 forgets the padding, 1,048 the new IP header and 1,052 the ICV.

questions.questionText: A VPN uses ESP in tunnel mode with a new 20-byte IPv4 header, the 8-byte ESP header, a 16-byte IV, a 16-byte ICV and AES blocks of 16 bytes (the encrypted part includes the 2-byte trailer). The path MTU is 1,492 bytes (PPPoE). What is the largest TCP MSS the inner hosts can use without fragmentation, assuming 20-byte inner IPv4 and TCP headers without options?
options: 1,390 bytes
1,382 bytes
1,452 bytes
1,398 bytes
questions.explanation: Room for the encrypted part: 1,492 − 20 − 8 − 16 − 16 = 1,432 bytes, rounded down to whole blocks = 1,424; the largest inner packet is 1,424 − 2 = 1,422 bytes, so MSS = 1,422 − 40 = 1,382 bytes. 1,390 skips the rounding to whole blocks, 1,398 leaves out the IV and 1,452 ignores IPsec altogether.

questions.questionText: A server sends a 100,000-byte file over TLS 1.3 with AES-128-GCM, filling each record with the maximum 16,384 bytes of plaintext. Each record adds a 5-byte header, a 1-byte inner content type and a 16-byte authentication tag, with no padding. How many bytes of TLS records are sent?
options: 100,154 bytes
100,147 bytes
100,035 bytes
100,022 bytes
questions.explanation: ceil(100,000 / 16,384) = 7 records (six of 16,384 bytes and one of 1,696), each with 5 + 1 + 16 = 22 bytes of overhead, so 100,000 + 7 × 22 = 100,154 bytes. 100,147 forgets the content-type byte, 100,035 counts only the headers and 100,022 ignores the 16,384-byte record limit.

questions.questionText: A 1,000-byte HTTP request is sent over TLS 1.3 (22 bytes of record overhead), TCP and IPv4 (20-byte headers each, no options). The resulting packet then goes through an ESP tunnel using AES-GCM: a new 20-byte IPv4 header, the 8-byte ESP header, an 8-byte IV and a 16-byte ICV, with padding only to make inner packet + padding + 2-byte trailer a multiple of 4 bytes (GCM needs no block padding). How long is the packet on the Internet?
options: 1,124 bytes
1,116 bytes
1,096 bytes
1,108 bytes
questions.explanation: Inner packet = 1,000 + 22 + 20 + 20 = 1,062 bytes; 1,062 + 2 = 1,064 is already a multiple of 4, so no padding; total = 20 + 8 + 8 + 1,064 + 16 = 1,116 bytes. 1,124 pads to 16-byte blocks as for CBC, 1,096 leaves out the new IP header and 1,108 the IV.

questions.questionText: An ESP receiver uses an anti-replay window of 64 packets. The highest sequence number received so far is 1000, and every number from 937 to 1000 has arrived except 950 and 960. Packets with these sequence numbers now arrive, in this order and all with valid ICVs: 950, 1000, 1040, 960, 1020. Which does the receiver accept?
options: 950, 1040 and 1020 are accepted; 1000 and 960 are dropped
950, 1040, 960 and 1020 are accepted; only 1000 is dropped
Only 1040 is accepted, because every packet numbered below the highest one seen is dropped
All five are accepted, because each has a valid ICV
questions.explanation: 950 lies in the window 937–1000 and is new, so it is accepted; 1000 is a duplicate; 1040 is new and moves the window to 977–1040. 960 now falls left of the window and is dropped even though it never arrived before, while 1020 is inside the window and new, so it is accepted.

subtopics.title: Wireless LAN Security & Firewalls
subtopics.subtitle: WEP flaws, WPA/WPA2/WPA3, firewall types and rules, DMZ, IDS vs IPS

concepts.text: Threats to Wireless LANs

Radio signals travel beyond walls, so anyone in range can capture WLAN frames without physical access. Typical threats are eavesdropping, unauthorised access (war driving), rogue access points and evil-twin APs that mimic a legitimate SSID, MAC address spoofing to bypass filters, deauthentication and jamming DoS attacks, and MITM. Hiding the SSID and MAC filtering are weak measures; real protection comes from strong authentication and encryption.
WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy)
How WEP (original IEEE 802.11, 1997) protects a frame:
items: A shared static key of 40 or 104 bits is concatenated with a 24-bit Initialisation Vector (IV) to form a 64 or 128-bit RC4 seed.
An Integrity Check Value ICV = CRC-32(M) is appended to the message.
The RC4 keystream is XORed with M || ICV; the IV is sent in clear with the frame.
Authentication is either open system or shared-key challenge-response.

concepts.text: Why WEP is broken:
items: The 24-bit IV gives only 2^24 (about 16.7 million) values, so IVs repeat quickly on a busy network, and a repeated IV means a repeated keystream.
Weak IVs leak key bytes through RC4's key scheduling (Fluhrer-Mantin-Shamir attack); tools recover the key within minutes.
CRC-32 is linear and unkeyed, so an attacker can flip bits and fix the ICV undetected.
No replay protection, no per-packet key and one static key shared by all users with no key management.

concepts.text: WPA, WPA2 and WPA3

WPA (2003) was an interim fix that ran on WEP hardware: it kept RC4 but added TKIP, which mixes a per-packet key, uses a 48-bit sequence counter against replay and adds the Michael MIC. WPA2 (IEEE 802.11i, 2004) replaced RC4 with AES in CCMP mode (counter mode for confidentiality plus CBC-MAC for integrity). Both work in Personal mode with a pre-shared key (PSK) or Enterprise mode using 802.1X/EAP with a RADIUS server, and derive session keys through a 4-way handshake. WPA3 (2018) replaces PSK with SAE.

rows: SAE (Dragonfly), forward secrecy, protected management frames

concepts.text: Firewalls

A firewall is a hardware or software system placed between a trusted internal network and an untrusted network such as the Internet. It enforces a security policy by examining traffic and allowing or blocking it according to rules. All traffic between the two networks must pass through it, and only authorised traffic may pass. Firewalls also log activity and can perform NAT.

rows: Each packet alone: source/destination IP, port, protocol, flags
Tracks connections in a state table; allows replies to established sessions
Relays and inspects content per application (HTTP, FTP, SMTP)
Validates TCP handshakes, then relays without inspecting content (SOCKS)
Stateful filtering plus application awareness, IPS, TLS inspection, user identity

concepts.text: Rules are checked top to bottom and the first match wins, so specific rules go before general ones and the last rule is usually an implicit default deny. Architectures: a screened host places a bastion host behind a packet-filtering router; a screened subnet puts a perimeter network, the DMZ (demilitarised zone), between an outer and an inner firewall (or a three-legged firewall). Public servers such as web, mail and DNS live in the DMZ, so if one is compromised the internal LAN is still protected.

rows: Out of band, watches a copy of traffic
Blocks or drops malicious traffic in real time
False positives can block legitimate traffic

concepts.text: Limitations of firewalls:
items: Cannot protect against attacks that bypass them (e.g. a user's own 4G modem or rogue AP).
Offer little protection against insider threats already inside the perimeter.
Cannot stop malware in allowed traffic or encrypted traffic unless they inspect content.
Cannot prevent social engineering such as phishing, and a misconfigured rule set can open holes.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Wi-Fi Security and Firewalls
Your notes on wireless security and firewalls, cleaned up and corrected:
items: WEP is the old, broken standard: never use it. WPA (with TKIP) was a stop-gap on WEP hardware, WPA2 (with AES-CCMP) is the long-standing standard, and WPA3 (with SAE) is the newest and strongest, so choose WPA3 or WPA2.

WEP is broken not because its key is short alone but because of design flaws: a 24-bit IV that soon repeats, a key-scheduling weakness in RC4, and an unkeyed CRC-32 integrity check that lets an attacker change bits undetected. Tools recover the key in minutes.

Correction: WPA2 does not encrypt with TKIP. TKIP is the WPA cipher; WPA2 uses AES in CCMP mode. WPA3 keeps AES, and in Personal mode it derives the master key with SAE instead of directly from the pre-shared key; the 4-way handshake still follows.

Personal (PSK) mode shares one passphrase for the whole network; Enterprise mode gives each user their own credentials through 802.1X with an authentication server (RADIUS) and EAP, so a leaver's access can be revoked without changing everyone's key.

A firewall is like a security guard at the boundary: it inspects traffic and allows or blocks it by a rule set. All traffic must pass through it, and only traffic the policy permits gets through; it also logs and can do NAT.

Firewall types from simple to deep: packet filter (layer 3-4 headers), stateful inspection (tracks connections), application/proxy gateway (layer 7, inspects content), and next-generation firewalls that add intrusion prevention and application awareness. A web application firewall (WAF) protects web servers against attacks such as SQL injection.

concepts.text:
How WEP builds one encrypted frame (and why it fails)
seed = IV (24 bits, sent in clear) || shared key K (40 or 104 bits)
keystream = RC4(seed)
ICV = CRC32(plaintext)                 (unkeyed, linear)
ciphertext = (plaintext || ICV) XOR keystream
Flaw 1: only 2^24 IVs, so two frames often share an IV and keystream;
        XOR the two ciphertexts and the keystream cancels out.
Flaw 2: RC4 weak-key IVs leak key bytes (Fluhrer-Mantin-Shamir).
Flaw 3: CRC32 is linear, so an attacker flips message bits and fixes
        the ICV to match, with no key: integrity is not protected.

concepts.plainText: WEP has N_IV = 2^24 = 16,777,216 distinct IVs; an AP that increments the IV by one for each frame at r frames per second reuses an IV after t_cycle = 2^24 / r seconds

rows: Personal: SAE (Dragonfly), forward secrecy; Enterprise: 802.1X/EAP; PMF required

concepts.text: The WPA2/WPA3 4-way handshake runs after authentication to prove that both sides know the pairwise master key (from the passphrase in Personal mode) and to derive fresh session keys. It exchanges nonces so that each session gets a different pairwise transient key, and it installs the group key for broadcast traffic. In WPA2-Personal an eavesdropper who captures the handshake can run an offline dictionary attack on the passphrase; WPA3's SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) fixes this by making each guess need a fresh online exchange and by giving forward secrecy, so a later passphrase compromise does not expose earlier traffic. The KRACK attack (2017), which replayed handshake messages to make a device reinstall a key already in use, was fixed by software patches, because WPA3 still runs the 4-way handshake after SAE.
Wireless attacks and weak defences to know:
items: Rogue access point: an unauthorised AP plugged into the network, opening a back door past the firewall.
Evil twin: an attacker's AP that copies a legitimate SSID (and often its look) to lure clients into associating, then runs a man-in-the-middle.

WPS PIN weakness: the 8-digit PIN is checked in two halves and its last digit is a checksum, so at most 10^4 + 10^3 = 11,000 guesses are needed instead of 10^7, letting the Reaver tool recover it in hours; disable WPS.
Deauthentication flood: forged 802.11 deauth frames knock clients off; protected management frames (PMF, mandatory in WPA3) stop this.
Weak measures: hiding the SSID and MAC-address filtering only slow a casual snooper, because the SSID still appears in client probes and MAC addresses are sent in clear and easily spoofed.

concepts.text:
Trace: a first-match rule table (top to bottom, then default deny)
R1 ALLOW  src 192.168.1.0/24  dst any            TCP 443
R2 ALLOW  src any            dst 203.0.113.10    TCP 80
R3 ALLOW  src 192.168.1.10   dst 192.168.2.0/24  TCP 22
R4 DENY   src any            dst any             TCP 23
R5 DENY   src 192.168.1.0/24 dst 203.0.113.10    TCP 80  (never reached)
P1 192.168.1.7 -> 203.0.113.10 : 80  -> R2 ALLOW (before R5)
P2 192.168.1.7 -> 8.8.8.8      : 443 -> R1 ALLOW
P3 192.168.1.7 -> 192.168.2.9  : 22  -> no rule -> default DENY
R5 is shadowed by R2, so put specific DENY rules above broad ALLOWs

rows: One packet's IP addresses, ports, protocol, flags
Connection state; replies to sessions started inside
Validity of the TCP handshake, then relays (e.g. SOCKS)
Full content of one protocol (HTTP, FTP, SMTP)
Above plus IPS, app and user awareness; WAF guards web apps

concepts.text: A demilitarised zone (DMZ) is a perimeter network between the Internet and the internal LAN, holding the servers that outsiders must reach (web, mail, DNS). A screened-subnet design puts it between an outer and an inner firewall, so that a compromised public server is still separated from the internal hosts. An intrusion detection system (IDS) sits out of band and only alerts on suspicious traffic, while an intrusion prevention system (IPS) sits inline and can drop it; both detect either by signatures (known patterns, which miss new attacks) or by anomalies (deviations from a learned baseline, which raise more false alarms). Network address translation (NAT) is not a firewall, but by hiding internal addresses behind one public address it blocks unsolicited inbound connections as a side effect.

Wi-Fi ladder: WEP (RC4 + 24-bit IV + CRC-32, broken) < WPA (TKIP) < WPA2 (AES-CCMP, 4-way handshake) < WPA3 (SAE, forward secrecy). PSK = one shared passphrase; Enterprise = 802.1X + EAP + RADIUS per user. Firewalls: packet filter L3-4, stateful adds a connection table, proxy L7. Rules are first-match with a default-deny at the end, so order matters. IDS detects, IPS (inline) blocks.

Common mistakes: saying WPA2 uses TKIP (that is WPA; WPA2 uses AES-CCMP) or that WEP's only fault is a short key; thinking a hidden SSID or MAC filtering gives real security; confusing IDS (alerts only) with IPS (blocks inline); and putting a broad ALLOW rule above a specific DENY, which leaves the DENY unreachable. A firewall cannot stop traffic that never passes through it, insider misuse, or malware inside allowed encrypted flows.

formulas.plainText: Frames for 50% chance of an IV repeat = 1.18 x sqrt(2^24), about 4823

notes.text: WEP = RC4 + 24-bit IV + CRC-32; WPA = TKIP; WPA2 = AES-CCMP; WPA3 = SAE. Packet filter works at L3-L4, application proxy at L7.
A stateful firewall can allow only reply packets that belong to connections initiated from inside, which a stateless packet filter cannot track.
An IDS only detects and alerts; it is an IPS, placed inline, that actually blocks traffic.

formulas.title: WEP encryption
formulas.description: WEP XORs the message and its CRC-32 ICV with an RC4 keystream seeded by the IV and shared key.

formulas.title: WEP IV space
formulas.description: The small 24-bit IV space makes IV and keystream reuse inevitable on a busy network.

formulas.title: Birthday bound for IV collision
formulas.description: With random IVs a repeat is more likely than not after only about 4800 frames.

flashcards.front: Which encryption does WPA2 use?
flashcards.back: AES in CCMP mode (counter mode with CBC-MAC), replacing WEP/WPA's RC4.

flashcards.front: Give three reasons WEP is insecure.
flashcards.back: Short 24-bit IV causes keystream reuse, weak RC4 IVs leak the key, and the linear CRC-32 ICV allows undetected modification.

flashcards.front: What is a DMZ?
flashcards.back: A perimeter subnet between an outer and inner firewall where public servers are placed, isolating them from the internal LAN.

flashcards.front: How does a circuit-level gateway differ from an application-level gateway?
flashcards.back: A circuit-level gateway validates TCP sessions and relays bytes without inspecting content; an application gateway understands and inspects the application protocol.

questions.questionText: WEP uses a 24-bit initialisation vector. How many distinct IV values are possible?
questions.explanation: 2^24 = 16,777,216; this small space causes IV and keystream reuse on busy networks.

questions.questionText: Which firewall keeps a table of active connections and allows incoming packets only if they belong to an established session?
options: Stateless packet filter
Stateful inspection firewall
Circuit-level gateway
Screened host router
questions.explanation: A stateful inspection firewall tracks connection state; a stateless packet filter judges each packet independently.

questions.questionText: In a screened-subnet firewall architecture, publicly accessible web and mail servers are normally placed in the:
options: DMZ between the outer and inner firewalls
Internal LAN behind the inner firewall
ISP's backbone network
Same VLAN as the users' workstations
questions.explanation: The DMZ exposes public services while keeping the internal network behind a second barrier if a DMZ server is compromised.

questions.questionText: What does WEP stand for in wireless LAN security?
options: Wireless Encrypted Protocol
Web Encryption Process
Wired Equivalent Privacy
Wireless Endpoint Protection
questions.explanation: WEP means Wired Equivalent Privacy: it aimed to give a wireless link privacy comparable to a wired one, but its design is broken and it must not be used.

questions.questionText: Which wireless security standard is the most secure?
options: WPA3
WPA
WPA2
WEP
questions.explanation: WPA3 (2018) is the newest and strongest: it uses SAE instead of a plain pre-shared key, adds forward secrecy and protected management frames, and resists offline dictionary attacks. WEP is broken and WPA is weak.

questions.questionText: What is the main purpose of a firewall in a network?
options: To resolve domain names into IP addresses
To encrypt every TCP connection end to end
To store the MAC addresses of every host on the LAN
To monitor and control incoming and outgoing traffic according to a security policy
questions.explanation: A firewall sits at a network boundary and allows or blocks traffic by a set of rules, so that only authorised traffic passes and the events are logged. Encryption, address tables and name resolution are the jobs of TLS/IPsec, switches and DNS.

questions.questionText: At which OSI layers can firewalls operate?
options: Only the physical layer
At several layers, depending on the type of firewall
Only the application layer
Only the network layer
questions.explanation: A packet filter works at layers 3-4, a proxy gateway at layer 7, a circuit-level gateway at layer 5 and a next-generation firewall across layers 3-7. So the layer depends on the firewall's type, not a single fixed layer.

questions.questionText: Which encryption does WPA2 use, and how does it differ from WPA?
options: WPA2 uses AES in CCMP mode, replacing the RC4-based TKIP that WPA introduced
WPA2 uses RC4 with TKIP, while WPA used DES
WPA2 uses WEP's RC4 with a longer key
WPA2 and WPA both use AES, differing only in key length
questions.explanation: WPA2 (IEEE 802.11i) mandates AES-CCMP, a modern block-cipher mode giving confidentiality and integrity. WPA was an interim scheme that kept RC4 but added TKIP so that it could run on existing WEP hardware.

questions.questionText: What is an evil-twin attack on a wireless network?
options: Sending forged deauthentication frames to disconnect clients
Guessing the Wi-Fi passphrase from a captured handshake
An attacker's access point that advertises the same SSID as a legitimate one, so that clients associate with it and their traffic can be intercepted
Flooding the channel with radio noise to cause a denial of service
questions.explanation: An evil twin impersonates a trusted network by copying its SSID (and often its captive portal), luring clients into connecting and enabling a man-in-the-middle. It is a rogue AP aimed specifically at mimicking a known network.

questions.questionText: Which statement about hiding the SSID and filtering by MAC address is correct?
options: Together they make a network as secure as WPA2
They are weak measures: the SSID still appears in client probe requests, and MAC addresses are sent in clear and easily spoofed
They encrypt the wireless traffic
They are required by the WPA3 standard
questions.explanation: Neither measure encrypts anything. A hidden SSID is revealed whenever a client looks for the network, and an attacker can sniff an allowed MAC address and clone it, so real security still comes from WPA2 or WPA3.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between an IDS and an IPS?
options: An IDS encrypts traffic, while an IPS decrypts it
An IDS works only on wireless networks and an IPS only on wired ones
An IDS is hardware and an IPS is always software
An IDS detects and alerts on suspicious traffic, usually out of band, while an IPS sits inline and can block or drop the malicious traffic in real time
questions.explanation: Both look for attacks by signatures or anomalies, but their placement and response differ: an IDS watches a copy of the traffic and raises alerts, whereas an inline IPS can stop the traffic, at the risk of blocking legitimate flows on a false positive.

questions.questionText: Why is WEP considered insecure, beyond simply having a short key?
options: It uses AES, which is too slow for wireless links
It requires a RADIUS server that most home routers lack
Its 24-bit IV soon repeats so keystreams are reused, RC4 has weak-key IVs that leak the key, and its unkeyed linear CRC-32 lets an attacker alter frames undetected
It encrypts the SSID, which breaks client discovery
questions.explanation: WEP's failures are structural: IV reuse exposes the keystream, the Fluhrer-Mantin-Shamir attack recovers the key from weak IVs, and the CRC-32 integrity check can be forged. Together these let tools break WEP within minutes.

questions.questionText: A study guide says WEP's main weakness is simply 'weak encryption keys that can be cracked easily'. Which more precise statement captures the real flaw?
options: The real flaw is the 24-bit IV: it is so small that IVs and keystreams repeat, and because it is sent in clear as the first bytes of the RC4 key, RC4's key-scheduling weakness reveals the key, however long the secret key is
WEP has no encryption at all, so frames travel in clear text
WEP keys expire after a few seconds and cannot be renewed
WEP uses AES-128, which has since been broken
questions.explanation: Even a 104-bit WEP key falls quickly, because the fault lies in the tiny clear-text IV, which makes keystreams repeat and exposes RC4's weakness to the FMS and PTW key-recovery attacks, not in the length of the secret. WEP does encrypt (with RC4), and it never used AES.

questions.questionText: How do WPA2/WPA3 Personal (PSK) and Enterprise modes differ?
options: Personal uses AES and Enterprise uses RC4
Personal encrypts the traffic and Enterprise leaves it in clear
Enterprise works only on wired networks
Personal shares one passphrase for the whole network, while Enterprise authenticates each user separately through 802.1X with EAP and a RADIUS server
questions.explanation: Both modes use the same AES-based encryption; they differ in authentication. Enterprise gives each user or device its own credentials via 802.1X/EAP and a RADIUS server, so access can be revoked individually without changing a shared passphrase.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the WPA2/WPA3 4-way handshake?
options: To scan for the least congested Wi-Fi channel
To let the client and access point confirm they share the master key and to derive fresh per-session keys, using exchanged nonces, and to install the group key
To assign the client an IP address
To negotiate the maximum data rate of the link
questions.explanation: The 4-way handshake runs after association: it proves both sides know the pairwise master key without sending it, mixes in nonces so each session gets a unique transient key, and delivers the group key for broadcasts. Channel selection, addressing and rates are separate.

questions.questionText: What advantage does WPA3's SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) have over the WPA2-Personal handshake?
options: Each password guess needs a fresh interaction with the access point, defeating offline dictionary attacks on captured handshakes, and it provides forward secrecy
It lets the network run without encryption
It doubles the Wi-Fi throughput
It removes the need for any password
questions.explanation: With WPA2-Personal an attacker who captures the 4-way handshake can try unlimited guesses offline. SAE makes every guess require a new online exchange with the AP and derives session keys so that a later password compromise does not expose earlier traffic.

questions.questionText: A basic packet-filtering firewall makes its decisions primarily using information from which OSI layers?
options: The physical layer only
The presentation layer
The network and transport layers (IP addresses, protocol, and TCP/UDP port numbers)
The data link layer only
questions.explanation: A packet filter inspects layer-3 and layer-4 header fields, source and destination IP addresses, the protocol, and the port numbers, to allow or deny each packet. Reading message content would need an application-layer (proxy) firewall.

questions.questionText: How does a stateful inspection firewall improve on a stateless packet filter?
options: It encrypts the packets it forwards
It keeps a table of active connections, so it can allow inbound packets only when they belong to a session already started from the trusted side
It works at the physical layer for higher speed
It stores a copy of every packet permanently for auditing
questions.explanation: A stateless filter judges each packet alone, so allowing replies means opening ports permanently. A stateful firewall remembers connections in a state table and lets return traffic through only while its session is active.

questions.questionText: Which firewall type inspects the actual content of an application protocol, so that it can, for example, block specific HTTP requests or filter FTP commands?
options: Stateless packet filter
Circuit-level gateway
Network address translation (NAT)
Application-level gateway (proxy firewall)
questions.explanation: An application-level gateway works at layer 7 and understands the protocol it relays, so it can inspect and filter the content itself. A circuit-level gateway only validates the TCP session and relays bytes without looking inside.

questions.questionText: What is the role of a web application firewall (WAF)?
options: It replaces TLS by encrypting web pages
It assigns IP addresses to web clients
It sits in front of web applications and filters HTTP requests to block attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting
It caches web pages to speed up delivery
questions.explanation: A WAF understands HTTP and web-application behaviour, so it can spot and block malicious requests aimed at the application layer, which a network firewall that only checks addresses and ports cannot. It complements, rather than replaces, TLS.

questions.questionText: Why is network address translation (NAT) often said to give a firewall-like side effect, even though it is not a firewall?
options: By mapping many private addresses to one public address, it has no entry for unsolicited inbound connections, so outside hosts cannot reach internal hosts directly unless a port is forwarded
It encrypts the payload of every packet that crosses it
It authenticates every user before allowing traffic
It inspects the application-layer content of each packet
questions.explanation: NAT keeps a table of connections started from inside; an unsolicited packet from outside matches no entry and is dropped. This blocks direct inbound access as a by-product, but NAT applies no security policy and inspects no content, so it is not a true firewall.

questions.questionText: Where should the publicly reachable web, mail and DNS servers be placed, and why?
options: Inside the ISP's network, so the company need not protect them
On the internal LAN with the workstations, for easier management
Directly on the Internet with no firewall, to maximise performance
In a DMZ, a perimeter network separated from the internal LAN, so that a compromised public server cannot directly reach the internal hosts
questions.explanation: Public servers must accept connections from outside, so they are the most exposed. Putting them in a DMZ between an outer and inner firewall means that if one is breached, the attacker is still separated from the internal network.

questions.questionText: A signature-based IDS/IPS and an anomaly-based one differ in a key way. Which statement is correct?
options: Signature-based detection catches brand-new (zero-day) attacks that anomaly-based detection misses

Signature-based detection matches known attack patterns, so it misses new attacks; anomaly-based detection flags deviations from a learned baseline, so it can catch new attacks but raises more false alarms
Anomaly-based detection needs a database of known attack signatures
Both methods can only be used in an IDS, never in an IPS
questions.explanation: A signature engine is accurate on known threats but blind to anything not yet in its database, while an anomaly engine can notice novel behaviour at the cost of more false positives. Either method can run in a detecting IDS or a blocking IPS.

questions.questionText: A network uses only MAC-address filtering and a hidden SSID, with open (unencrypted) Wi-Fi. What is the security result?
options: Weak: an attacker sniffs the SSID from probe traffic, copies an allowed MAC address seen in clear, and reads all traffic because there is no encryption
Strong, because two independent controls are combined
Adequate for confidential data, because the SSID is hidden
Secure against eavesdropping but not against denial of service
questions.explanation: None of these measures encrypts the air link, so anyone in range reads the frames; the SSID leaks in management frames and MAC addresses are trivial to spoof. Only WPA2 or WPA3 encryption gives real protection.

questions.questionText:
A firewall evaluates rules top to bottom, first match wins, with an implicit default deny at the end:
R1 ALLOW src 192.168.1.0/24 any TCP 443
R2 ALLOW src any dst 203.0.113.10 TCP 80
R3 ALLOW src 192.168.1.10 dst 192.168.2.0/24 TCP 22
R4 DENY src any any TCP 23
What happens to a packet from 192.168.1.50 to 192.168.2.20 on TCP port 22?
options: Allowed by R3
Allowed by R1
Denied by the default rule
Denied by R4
questions.explanation: R1 needs port 443, R2 needs destination 203.0.113.10, R3 needs source 192.168.1.10 (not .50) and R4 needs port 23, so none matches. With first-match evaluation the packet falls through to the implicit default deny.

questions.questionText: Using the same rule set (R1 ALLOW 192.168.1.0/24 -> any TCP 443; R2 ALLOW any -> 203.0.113.10 TCP 80; R3 ALLOW 192.168.1.10 -> 192.168.2.0/24 TCP 22; R4 DENY any -> any TCP 23; then default deny), how is a packet from 192.168.1.50 to 203.0.113.10 on TCP port 80 handled?
options: Denied by the default rule
Allowed by R2
Denied by R4
Allowed by R1
questions.explanation: R1 requires port 443, so it does not match a port-80 packet; the next rule, R2, allows any source to reach 203.0.113.10 on TCP 80, so the packet is allowed there. First-match means later rules are not consulted.

questions.questionText: An administrator adds, at the bottom of a first-match rule set, R5 DENY src 192.168.1.0/24 dst 203.0.113.10 TCP 80, intending to stop internal users reaching the DMZ web server, but R2 ALLOW src any dst 203.0.113.10 TCP 80 already sits above it. What is the effect, and how should it be fixed?
options: R5 works as intended, because a DENY rule always overrides an ALLOW
R5 blocks all traffic to 203.0.113.10, including from outside
Both rules fire, so the packets are logged twice but still allowed
R5 is never reached, because R2 matches those packets first; the specific DENY must be placed above the broad ALLOW
questions.explanation: With first-match evaluation, an internal-to-DMZ port-80 packet matches R2 and is allowed before R5 is ever examined, so R5 is shadowed and useless. Specific rules must come before more general ones in the list.

questions.questionText: A WPS-enabled router uses an 8-digit PIN. The router validates the PIN in two halves and the last digit is only a checksum computed from the first seven, so the first half is 4 digits and the second effective half is 3 digits. What is the worst-case number of online guesses to recover the PIN, and how does that compare with brute-forcing all 8 digits?
options: 100,000,000 guesses, the same as brute force
10,000,000 guesses, the same as brute force
11,000 guesses, versus 100,000,000 for all 8 digits
1,100 guesses, versus 10,000,000 for 7 digits
questions.explanation: Splitting the check lets the halves be found independently: at most 10^4 = 10,000 for the first half and 10^3 = 1,000 for the second (the eighth digit is a checksum), giving 11,000 tries instead of 10^8. This design flaw is why the Reaver tool can crack WPS, and why WPS should be disabled.

questions.questionText: A WEP access point increments the 24-bit IV by one for every frame and transmits 500 frames per second. Approximately how long until it is forced to reuse an IV by cycling through the whole IV space?
options: About 9.3 hours
About 4.7 hours
About 2.2 minutes
About 18.6 hours
questions.explanation: The IV has 2^24 = 16,777,216 values, so a full cycle takes 16,777,216 / 500 = 33,554 s = 9.32 hours. 4.7 hours assumes 1,000 frames/s, 2.2 minutes wrongly uses a 16-bit IV, and reuse actually begins far sooner because of random collisions.

questions.questionText: A home network has WPS enabled with WPA2-Personal and a long, random passphrase. Why is the network still at serious risk, and what is the best fix?
options: The long passphrase is the weakness; shorten it so the 4-way handshake is faster
The risk is only that neighbours see the SSID; hide the SSID to fix it
There is no real risk, because WPA2 with a long passphrase cannot be broken
WPS lets an attacker recover the router's PIN in about 11,000 online tries and from it obtain the WPA2 passphrase, so the strong passphrase is bypassed; disable WPS
questions.explanation: The WPS PIN can be brute-forced in roughly 11,000 attempts because it is checked in two halves, and recovering it yields the WPA2 key no matter how strong the passphrase is. The remedy is to turn WPS off, not to change the passphrase.

questions.questionText: An organisation wants outsiders to reach its web server but must keep the internal LAN protected even if that server is hacked, and it wants to block and log intrusion attempts inline. Which design best meets these goals?
options: Place the web server on the internal LAN and rely on NAT alone
Put the web server in a DMZ between an outer and inner firewall, and deploy an inline IPS to detect and drop malicious traffic
Expose the web server directly on the Internet and install an IDS that only sends alerts
Use a hidden SSID and MAC filtering on the server's switch port
questions.explanation: The DMZ isolates the exposed server so a breach does not reach internal hosts, and an inline IPS both detects and actively blocks attacks, unlike an IDS that only alerts. NAT and Wi-Fi measures do not meet these requirements.

questions.questionText: What is a rogue access point, and why is it dangerous?
options: An unauthorised access point connected to the internal network, which opens a wireless back door that bypasses the perimeter firewall
An access point that has simply lost power, so clients cannot connect
A vendor's default access point that ships with WPA3 enabled
An access point that broadcasts on a licensed frequency by mistake
questions.explanation: A rogue AP is an unsanctioned device, often plugged in by an insider for convenience, that lets attackers onto the internal LAN behind the firewall. It differs from an evil twin, which impersonates a known SSID to trap clients.

questions.questionText: An attacker floods a Wi-Fi network with forged 802.11 deauthentication frames, repeatedly knocking clients off the network. Which feature, mandatory in WPA3, prevents this?
options: Hiding the SSID
MAC address filtering
Protected Management Frames (PMF, 802.11w), which authenticate management frames so forged deauth frames are rejected
A longer pre-shared key
questions.explanation: Classic 802.11 management frames, including deauthentication, are unauthenticated, so anyone can forge them to disconnect clients. PMF authenticates these frames; it is optional in WPA2 but required in WPA3.
